The 12-Layer Trimer-Based Hexagonal Perovskite Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12

Teresa Lee1, Xianghan Xu1, Weiwei Xie2, and Robert J. Cava1*

1Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544

2Department of Chemistry, Michigan State University, East Lansing, MI 48824

*Author to whom correspondence should be addressed. Email: rcava@princeton.edu

## Abstract

We describe the crystal structure and basic magnetic properties of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12, a

previously unreported twelve layer (12L-) hexagonal (R-3m) chloride perovskite. Its crystal

structure features face sharing MnCl6 octahedra that form Mn3Cl12 trimers. The trimers, which

form a triangular array, are separated by corner sharing to layers of disordered single Ca(Mn)Cl6

octahedra. The decreased intratrimer Mn-Mn distance yields stronger magnetic coupling within

trimers than between trimers. The dominant magnetic interactions are antiferromagnetic ( = -

105 K), the effective magnetic moment per Mn2+ is 6.5 , and potential signatures of magnetic

frustration are observed. Behavior consistent with short- and long-range magnetic order is

exhibited at approximately 37 and 0.7 K, respectively.

Keywords: 12L-hexagonal perovskite, halide perovskite, magnetism, magnetic trimers

## 1. Introduction

The trimer-based Ba4NbTM3O12 (TM= Mn, Ru, Rh, and Ir) and Ba4LnRu3O12 (Ln= Tb-

Lu) oxides have garnered significant interest in recent years owing to their interesting magnetic

properties, which emerge in part as a result of their crystal structures.1–5 These materials

crystallize as hexagonal perovskites possessing a triangular array of magnetic face-sharing

TM3O12 trimers connected by corner sharing to Ln/NbO6 octahedra, and are termed “12L-

hexagonal perovskites” due to being built from three units that are four octahedra (the trimer plus

the bridging octahedron) high. Their magnetic properties are governed by the inter- and

intratrimer interactions, wherein the trimers themselves act as either “molecular” or “point

charge” systems.2,6 In the former case, electrons in the trimer are delocalized, while in the latter

they are localized at the transition metal sites.6 The distinction between the two can typically be

determined experimentally based on the calculated value of the effective magnetic moment, as

the formation of molecular orbitals yields less unpaired electrons per unit and, in turn, a

markedly smaller effective magnetic moment than would result from an independent transition

metal ion.

Within this specific family of 12L-hexagonal oxide perovskites, the triangular

arrangement of the TM trimers yields the potential for geometric magnetic frustration, which is

observed in the Ba4NbTM3O12 variants where TM= Ru and Mn.1,3 Moreover, Ba4Nb0.8Ir3.2O12—

a disordered analog of Ba4NbIr3O12—was reported, wherein the Nb site is partially occupied by

both Nb (0.8) and Ir (0.2).7,8 Both the stoichiometric  and nonstoichiometric versions were found

to potentially host a quantum spin-liquid state.2,7 A non-magnetic isostructural fluoride version

of these materials, Cs4CaMg3F12, is also known.9

Having a different formula and octahedron ordering scheme, the A2BB’X6 (A= Cs or an

organic cation; B=Na, K, Ag, or Tl; B’=In, Sb, Bi, or a rare-earth metal; and X=Cl, Br, or I)

hexagonal perovskites10 also consist of 12 layers of octahedra. Charge neutrality for this phase

requires B to be a monovalent metal and B’ to be a trivalent metal. These materials form trimers

of B-B’-B face-sharing octahedra connected by corner sharing B’X6 octahedra. While A2BB’X6

compounds are of interest for their potential roles as Pb-free photovoltaic alternatives,11,12 they

are typically nonmagnetic. One magnetic variant possessing this structure-type is that of

Cs2AgCrCl6, where the Cr3+ B’ ion is magnetic, and is located between the non-magnetic AgCl6

octahedra in the trimers. This breaks up the potential magnetic trimer, making the compounds act

like they contain individual layers of magnetic and non-magnetic octahedra. As a result,

Cs2AgCrCl6 was found to be paramagnetic, consistent with the expected behavior of isolated

Cr3+ ions.10

The related phase CsMnCl3 crystallizes in the R-3m space group and possesses a 9L-

structure rather than a 12L structure.13 This material features octahedron-based Mn3Cl12 trimers

connected to one another via corner sharing, with no intermediate layers of octahedra. Neutron

diffraction and magnetization measurements indicate that CsMnCl3 exhibits long-range

antiferromagnetic ordering at 67 K.14,15

The physical properties observed in the Ba4NbTM3O12 and Ba4LnRu3O12 compounds and

the prospect of isostructural halide compounds motivated our synthesis and magnetic

characterization of a phase of potential composition Cs4CaTM3X12, in hopes of uncovering a new


<!-- Page 3 -->


material with attractive magnetic properties. To this end, in the current study we report our

synthesis of the 12L-hexagonal perovskite Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12, a manganese-rich version of the

ideal Cs4CaMn3Cl12 formula, which is isostructural to the Ba4NbTM3O12 and Ba4LnRu3O12

materials as well as to Cs4CaMg3F12. Through magnetic susceptibility and heat capacity

measurements, we find that the dominant magnetic interactions are antiferromagnetic, observe

potential signatures of magnetic frustration, and find that this material exhibits behavior that is

consistent with the appearance of short-range magnetic ordering at about 37 K and long-range

ordering at approximately 0.7 K.

## 2. Experimental

2.1. Synthesis and Structural Characterization

Single crystals of Cs4Ca0.8Mn3.2Cl12 were obtained via a melt of a 2:1:1 mixture of

anhydrous CsCl, anhydrous MnCl2, and vacuum oven dried CaCl2·2H2O (Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%;

Sigma Aldrich, 99.99%; and EM Science, 99.5%, respectively). The reagents were ground

together with a mortar and pestle and subsequently heated at 600℃ overnight in a furnace in an

evacuated quartz tube. The tube was then cooled to room temperature at 10℃/hour.

Single phase polycrystalline Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 was synthesized using CsCaCl3 and

CsMnCl3 as precursors. These end members were formed by first melting stoichiometric

amounts of CsCl and MCl2 (M= Ca or Mn) in evacuated quartz tubes (heated overnight to 915℃

for M=Ca and 700℃ for M=Mn). The tubes were then cooled at approximately 10℃/hour and

75℃/hour for M=Mn and M=Ca, respectively. Material made at the ideal composition,

Cs4CaMn3Cl12, was found to contain multiple phases. However, CsCaCl3 and CsMnCl3 in the

0.7:3.3 mole ratio yielded single phase material when ground with a mortar and pestle and heated

in an evacuated quartz tube to 510℃. The compound was heated at this temperature overnight

and was then allowed to cool to room temperature. The mixture was then ground with a mortar

and pestle and the above process was repeated, heating to 515℃ and again to 550℃, where it was

annealed for three days. The resulting powder was a very light pink. Due to the hygroscopic

nature of the material, all syntheses and subsequent analyses were performed in a N2-filled

glovebox.

The phase purity and crystal structure of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 was determined via both

single crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) using a Bruker D8 Quest Eco diffractometer with a


<!-- Page 4 -->


Photon 2 CPAD detector using graphite monochromated Mo K radiation ( = 0.71073 Å) under

a flowing N2 stream to prevent decomposition in air and powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) using

a Bruker D8 ADVANCE Eco with Cu K radiation ( = 1.5406 Å) and a LynxEye-XE detector.

A crystal was selected from the Mn-rich region of the melt and its SCXRD data was collected at

295 K. The frames were integrated with the SAINT program within the APEX III program,

version 2017.3-0. The crystal structure was determined using OLEX2 GUI,16 in which the

structure was solved with the SHEL XT17 structure solution program using intrinsic phasing and

refined with the SHEL XL18 refinement package using least-squares minimization. Both Ca2+

and Mn2+ ions were constrained to the 3a position and their occupancies were freely refined. The

best refinement resulted from a disordered 3a site, occupied by 20% Mn2+ and 80% Ca2+,

yielding the formula Cs4Ca0.8Mn3.2Cl12. However, we were unable to make polycrystalline

samples at this ratio of Ca to Mn without observing impurities in our PXRD pattern. Thus, for

the current study we deferred to the more Mn-rich composition Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12, which we

synthesized in polycrystalline form without any discernible impurities. Attempts to deviate from

this stoichiometry are described in the Supplementary Data, Figure S1. We have no theoretical or

experimental explanation for why this composition is stable under our synthetic conditions, but

note that non-whole number formulas can sometimes be observed in oxide materials. A more

detailed analysis of various refinement attempts is included in Table S1, and preliminary energy

dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) data is presented in Figure S2 and Table S2. The crystal

structure acquired from the SCXRD solution served as a starting model for the Rietveld

refinement performed on PXRD data using GSAS II.19 The occupancies for the Mn2+ and Ca2+

ions sharing the 3a site were fixed to 0.3 and 0.7, respectively, to yield the single phase

composition. VESTA20 software enabled the visualization of the crystal structure.

2.2. Magnetic and Thermodynamic Characterization

A Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) equipped with a

vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM) was utilized to measure the magnetization of a

polycrystalline sample of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12. The magnetization was measured as a function of

both temperature and applied magnetic field. Magnetic susceptibility (defined as M/H; where M

is the sample magnetization and H is the applied magnetic field in Oe) data was collected with

applied fields of 20 and 50 Oe. In order to evaluate the magnetic properties of the material, the

## 3. Results and Discussion

3.1. Crystal Structure

The SCXRD analysis and subsequent Rietveld evaluation of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 reveals

that this material crystallizes in the rhombohedral R-3m (No. 166) space group, adopting the

12L-hexagonal perovskite structure. Figure 1 illustrates the PXRD pattern and structural

refinement for Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12. The structural and lattice parameters obtained from the

Rietveld refinement are detailed in Table 1, and Figure 2 depicts the crystal structure.

This material is isostructural to the oxide variants Ba4NbTM3O12 (TM = Mn, Ru, Rh, Ir)1–

3 and Ba4LnRu3O12 (Ln = Tb-Lu)4,5 as well as the fluoride compound Cs4Mg3CaF12.9 More

specifically, Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 possesses a disordered 3a site, which is partially occupied by both

Ca2+ and Mn2+ (Figure 2). This disorder on the 3a position has also been observed for

Ba4Nb0.8Ir3.2O12.7,8  Thus, the title compound features layers of face-sharing Mn3Cl12 trimers (the

6c and 3b sites) connected by corner-sharing Ca(Mn)Cl6 octahedra (the 3a sites). The Mn-trimers

form a triangular array and, along with the Ca(Mn)Cl6 octahedra, stack along the

crystallographic c-axis to generate the 12-layer rhombohedral unit cell. The single-crystal

refinement data are presented in Table S3, and the atomic coordinates obtained from the SCXRD

solution are presented in Table S4.

The magnetic and thermodynamic properties of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 were investigated on a

polycrystalline sample. Because both Cs+ and Ca2+ are nonmagnetic, the magnetism arises solely

from the Mn2+ ions. The intratrimer Mn-Mn distance is 3.202(7) Å while the intertrimer Mn-Mn

distance is 7.36213(18) Å. Thus, the dominant magnetic interactions likely originate from within

the trimers as opposed to between trimers. Despite the relatively small intratrimer Mn-Mn

distance, Mn2+ ions within a trimer are not as close to one another as they are in Ba4NbMn3O12

(intratrimer Mn-Mn distance of 2.4694(1) Å), for example, in which the Mn-trimers are

hypothesized to behave as molecular units rather than as point charges (however, note that the

trimers in Ba4NbMn3O12 are composed of two Mn4+ ions and one Mn3+ ion).3 Spin information is

communicated by the Mn2+ ions within each trimer via a Mn-Cl-Mn superexchange mechanism.

The end members of the Mn-trimers are separated from the disordered Mn/Ca site (which they

are connected to via corner sharing) by 5.147(4) Å, and can likewise interact with the Mn, when

present in the 3a position, via a Mn-Cl-Mn superexchange pathway. Intertrimer interactions

occur through a Mn-Cl-Cl-Mn super-superexchange process. The temperature-dependent

magnetic susceptibility (zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC)) for applied magnetic


<!-- Page 8 -->


fields of 50 and 20 Oe is depicted in Figure 3a and 3b, respectively. Figure 3a also features the

inverse susceptibility data collected at 50 Oe.

Although the experimental effective magnetic moment value of 6.47  per Mn2+ is

larger than that of the theoretical spin-only value for an isolated Mn2+ ion in an octahedral

environment (5.92 ),22 several studies regarding the magnetic properties of CsMnCl3, which

also possesses Mn trimers, have reported  values of 6.35 and 6.37 , respectively.15,23

Because the experimental effective magnetic moment is comparable to that of the spin-only

moment of high-spin Mn2+, it is likely that the Mn2+ ions within each trimer behave

independently as point charge systems, rather than as “molecular” units. As previously stated,

this notion is also supported by the fact that the Mn2+ ions within the trimers are sufficiently far

from each other, so as to discourage molecular behavior. In contrast, the effective magnetic

moment determined for Ba4NbMn3O12 (4.82 ) is smaller than the theoretical values of 6.16 

(for low-spin Mn3+) and 7.35  (for high-spin Mn3+), suggesting that the Mn ions within each

trimer create a Mn “molecule”.3 The temperature extracted from the derivative curve in Figure

3b (approximately 37.4 K) likely represents the onset of short-range magnetic ordering, such as

would be found for intratrimer coupling.

The magnetization was measured from 0-9 T (1 T = 10,000 Oe·) at 1.8, 5, 13.5, 25, and

75 K. At 1.8 K—below the temperature of the short-range ordering—the material exhibits a

ferromagnetic contribution to its magnetization, which is confirmed by the low-field hysteresis

themselves into an antiparallel arrangement, until approximately 2.2 T where they resume their

parallel alignment up to 9 T. The linear behavior exhibited at 75 K, which is well above the

temperature of the transition, is characteristic of the normal response of a paramagnetic system to

an applied magnetic field. The seemingly-ferromagnetic components present in both the

temperature- and field-dependent susceptibility data might also be explained by canted

confirm this assignment.

The absence of a clear anomaly in the heat capacity data (Figure 5a,b) suggests that the material

does not undergo a three-dimensional magnetic phase transition until around 0.7 K. On the other

hand, short-range ordering—such as intratrimer interactions—does not typically manifest as

peaks in heat capacity data. Indeed, the broad peak in the Cmag/T versus temperature plot (Figure

5c) is characteristic of short-range ordering as opposed to long-range correlations. Therefore, the

susceptibility and magnetization analysis in tandem with the heat capacity data allows us to infer

that Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 exhibits short-range magnetic coupling beginning at approximately 37.4

K. Moreover, the sharp peak at 0.7 K (Figure 5b,c) likely denotes long-range magnetic ordering.

The final magnetic entropy per Mn2+ ion is 5.15 J·mol-1·K-1, which is much smaller than the

theoretical S=Rln(2S+1) value of 14.9 J·mol-1·K-1 expected for Heisenberg spins that are fully 3D

ordered. Rather, this value is consistent with the theoretical S=Rln2 value of 5.76 J·mol-1·K-1

expected for Ising spins that are fully 3D ordered. More in-depth characterization, such as

neutron diffraction at different temperatures, would enable confirmation of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12’s

magnetic structure and is therefore of interest for further studies.

In order to unambiguously show that our material is distinct from CsMnCl3, we also

synthesized CsMnCl3 (synthesis details included in the Experimental section). The experimental

PXRD pattern for our CsMnCl3 is detailed in Figure S4 and a comparison of the PXRD patterns

of Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 and CsMnCl3 is illustrated in Figure S5. The magnetic susceptibility and

zero-field heat capacity data for CsMnCl3 are included in Figure S6. Our CsMnCl3 orders


<!-- Page 13 -->


antiferromagnetically at 67 K, in agreement with previous reports,14,15 and there is no indication

in our magnetic susceptibility or heat capacity data that any of this material is present in our

samples. The dissimilarities in the crystal structures, magnetic susceptibilities, and heat

capacities of the two materials instills confidence that the title compound is indeed entirely

different from CsMnCl3.

## 4. Conclusions

The previously unreported halide hexagonal perovskite Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 was

synthesized via a solid state reaction. Through SCXRD analysis and a powder Rietveld

refinement, we find that this material crystallizes in the R-3m (No. 166) space group, belonging

to the 12L-hexagonal perovskite family, and possesses Mn3Cl12 trimers connected by Ca(Mn)Cl6

octahedra. The magnetic effects are governed by intra- and intertrimer interactions, and the

shorter intratrimer Mn2+-Mn2+ distance compared to the intertrimer Mn2+-Mn2+ distance

promotes intratrimer over intertrimer coupling. Temperature and field-dependent magnetic

susceptibility measurements reveal the dominance of antiferromagnetic coupling, with a 

value of -105 K. The triangular array of the Mn-trimers yields the possibility for geometric

magnetic frustration, which may suppress the three-dimensional ordering. We discern a magnetic

phase transition in the 	 versus T data at approximately 37 K and infer that this is a signature of

short-range magnetic ordering as opposed to long-range ordering. An anomaly in the heat

capacity data at 0.7 K likely designates long-range ordering within the material. Our synthesis of

the novel chloride compound Cs4Ca0.7Mn3.3Cl12 encourages the search for isostructural halide

compounds possessing complex magnetic effects.
